extracted.intended_audience: graduate students or advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Foundational criteria, definitions, and checks for properties of schemes (Noetherian, integral, normal, factorial, finite type, varieties) and for quasicoherent OX-modules, together with exercises and examples illustrating how to verify these properties in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying topological space of a Noetherian scheme is Noetherian
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a Noetherian scheme then its underlying topological space is Noetherian; consequently all open subsets of a Noetherian scheme are quasicompact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference: Exercise 5.1.C and Exercise 3.6.U. Use this to deduce quasicompactness of open sets in Noetherian schemes; remember 'Noetherian' here refers to the scheme being Noetherian (locally Noetherian + quasicompact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally Noetherian implies quasiseparated
rubrics_metrics.description: Locally Noetherian schemes are quasiseparated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as Exercise 5.3.A. This gives a quick way to verify quasiseparatedness in the frequently-encountered locally finite type / Noetherian contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of irreducible/connected components for Noetherian schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noetherian scheme has a finite number of irreducible components; it also has a finite number of connected components, each a finite union of irreducible components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.3.B; hints refer to Proposition 3.6.15. Use the Noetherian hypothesis to avoid infinite decompositions; this is used later in arguments that reduce checks to closed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of an integral scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noetherian scheme X is integral if and only if X is nonempty and connected and all stalks O_{X,p} are integral domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.3.C. Use that integral = irreducible + reduced and that reducedness is stalk-local; for locally Noetherian schemes one can extend the argument via covers by open irreducible subsets. Note: some Noetherian hypotheses are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of A-scheme (scheme over a ring A)
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-scheme is a scheme where all rings of sections of the structure sheaf (over all open sets) are A-algebras and all restriction maps are maps of A-algebras; equivalently (later) a morphism X → Spec A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the relative notion of a scheme over a base ring A and underpins definitions like 'locally of finite type over A' and 'finite type over A'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally finite type and finite type A-schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: X is locally of finite type over A if it can be covered by affine opens Spec B_i where each B_i is a finitely generated A-algebra. If X is furthermore quasicompact, it is of finite type over A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology is cumbersome until morphisms are introduced; practical examples: Spec C[x1,...,xn]/I and P^n_C are finite type over C. If base A is Noetherian, locally finite type implies locally Noetherian; finite type over a Noetherian ring implies Noetherian scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiprojective and open subschemes of projective schemes give finite type
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Any quasiprojective A-scheme is of finite type over A; if A is Noetherian then it is a Noetherian scheme. (b) An open subscheme U of a projective A-scheme is locally of finite type over A; if A is Noetherian then U is quasicompact and hence quasiprojective and of finite type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.3.D. Part (b) warns that quasicompactness of an open need not hold when A is non-Noetherian and asks for counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of (affine/quasi)projective k-variety
rubrics_metrics.description: An affine scheme that is reduced and of finite type over k is an affine k-variety. A reduced (quasi)projective k-scheme is a (quasi)projective k-variety. (Literature sometimes requires irreducibility or algebraically closed base field in the definition.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.3.7 and warning: conventions vary; know the author's convention and check when irreducibility or algebraic closure of k is assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a closed point
rubrics_metrics.description: For a locally finite type k-scheme, the degree of a closed point p is the degree [κ(p):k] of the residue field extension. If k is algebraically closed, every closed point has degree 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.3.8; used for counting points and in arithmetic geometry arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of normal scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme X is normal if all stalks O_{X,p} are integrally closed integral domains (i.e., integrally closed in their fraction fields). Normality is a stalk-local property; normal schemes are reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 5.4.1. Use this as the working definition; later results (e.g., Hartogs-type extension phenomena) use normality. For rings, 'normal ring' often means Spec A is normal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking normality via localization and closed points
rubrics_metrics.description: Integral closedness is preserved under localization: if A is integrally closed then S^{-1}A is integrally closed. For quasicompact or locally finite type schemes, normality can be checked at closed points because each point is a generization of a closed point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.4.A and surrounding discussion. This provides practical reduction in verifications: check normality on maximal ideals/closed points rather than every point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of integral-closedness local/global (Prop. 5.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an integral domain A, the following are equivalent: (i) A is integrally closed; (ii) A_p is integrally closed for all prime ideals p; (iii) A_m is integrally closed for all maximal ideals m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use localization arguments and the ideal-of-denominators trick in the proof; this justifies checking integral-closedness locally at maximal ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of factoriality (scheme-level UFD condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme X is factorial if all of its stalks are unique factorization domains (UFDs). Equivalently, every local ring of X is a UFD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 5.4.3. Note: Spec A factorial does not necessarily imply A is a UFD, and conversely. Use affine covers of UFDs to show factoriality in many examples, but beware pathological counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between UFD and factoriality; how to check UFD
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a UFD then Spec A is factorial; conversely, factorial schemes need not be the Spec of a UFD. Practical checks for a Noetherian integral domain being a UFD include: Euclidean algorithm (elementary), localization of a UFD is a UFD, height-1 primes principal, being normal with class group Cl = 0, and Nagata's Lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 5.4.5. Use these criteria as tools; caution that power series extensions may fail UFD property even when A is UFD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factoriality implies normality; UFDs are integrally closed
rubrics_metrics.description: Unique factorization domains are integrally closed; hence factorial schemes are normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.4.F (important). Use this to deduce normality quickly from factoriality; but normality need not imply factoriality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and counterexamples for normality and UFD-ness
rubrics_metrics.description: A variety of explicit examples are given (Spec Z, A^n_k, P^n_k, certain quadratic cones, Z[√−5], cones over quadric surfaces) showing when rings/schemes are normal, integrally closed but not UFD, factorial but not coming from a UFD, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 5.4.G — 5.4.N provide concrete constructions and hints. These examples are essential anti-patterns and test-cases when applying the abstract criteria above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of quasicoherent sheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: An O_X-module F is quasicoherent if for every affine open Spec A ⊂ X, the restriction F|_{Spec A} is isomorphic to the sheaf associated to some A-module M (i.e., F|_{Spec A} ≅ ~M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 6.1.1. This is the primary local characterization of quasicoherence; one typically checks this on an affine open cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of quasicoherence with checking on an affine cover (Theorem 6.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The property 'F|_{Spec A} ≅ ~M for some A-module M' satisfies the hypotheses of the Affine Communication Lemma, so to check quasicoherence it suffices to verify this property on a collection of affine open sets covering X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem allows practical checking of quasicoherence by verifying local models on an affine cover and then gluing; see proof for explicit gluing using kernels of maps of modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gluing modules to produce global quasicoherent sheaves (construction via kernel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given O_{Spec A}-module data (M_i on distinguished opens Spec A_{f_i} and isomorphisms on overlaps satisfying cocycle conditions), one can reconstruct a global A-module M as ormula M = ker(γ) where γ encodes differences on overlaps; then ~M restricts to the given local modules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equations (6.1.2.1)-(6.1.2.4) and Exercise 6.1.A. This is the practical gluing construction used to show equivalence Mod_A ≃ QCoh(Spec A) and to prove descent statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasicoherent sheaves satisfy faithfully flat descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark (for experts): the proof of Theorem 6.1.2, phrased carefully, shows that quasicoherent sheaves satisfy faithfully flat descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind when using flat covers or descent arguments for quasicoherent sheaves in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguished affine base captures sheaf data
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinguished affine base (affine open sets and distinguished inclusions) suffices to recover sheaves on X: a sheaf on this base determines a unique sheaf on X and morphisms between such sheaves correspond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 6.2.1 and Theorem 6.2.2. Use this to reduce global sheaf-theoretic questions to checking data and restrictions only on affine opens and distinguished inclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of quasicoherence via localization of sections (Very Important)
rubrics_metrics.description: An O_X-module F is quasicoherent if and only if for every distinguished inclusion Spec A_f ⊂ Spec A the natural map α : Γ(Spec A, F) actored→ Γ(Spec A, F)  oisomorphic→ Γ(Spec A_f, F) (equivalently Γ(Spec A, F)  ≅ Γ(Spec A_f, F)) is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 6.2.D (labeled VERY IMPORTANT). This is the most practical and frequently-used characterization: sections on distinguished affines are given by localizing the module of sections on the bigger affine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor products of quasicoherent sheaves computed on affines
rubrics_metrics.description: If F and G are quasicoherent and on an affine Spec A we have Γ(Spec A, F) = M and Γ(Spec A, G) = N, then Γ(Spec A, F ⊗ G) ≅ M ⊗_A N, and restriction maps correspond to the expected localization maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 6.2.F. This allows computations of tensor products and related constructions by working entirely on affine opens without additional sheafification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torsion-free and torsion quasicoherent sheaves (stalk-local notions)
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-module M is torsion-free if am=0 implies a is a zerodivisor or m=0; for integral domains this means am=0 only if a=0 or m=0. An O_X-module F is torsion-free if all stalks F_p are torsion-free. On a reduced scheme, a quasicoherent sheaf is torsion if its stalk at the generic point of every irreducible component is 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 6.1.4 and 6.1.5. Use these notions when classifying subsheaves, and in curve/coherent-sheaf contexts where torsion is particularly simple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of sheaf of nilpotents as a quasicoherent ideal sheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a ring, then N(A_f) ≅ N(A)_f; using this, one can define the quasicoherent sheaf of nilpotents on any scheme X (an ideal sheaf of O_X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 6.2.E. This is an example showing that many natural ideal-type constructions are quasicoherent and behave well under localization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness of X_f and use of X_f in constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: For f ∈ Γ(X,O_X), the locus X_f where f does not vanish is open (notation X_f avoids implying X affine); these opens behave like distinguished affines in various arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 6.2.7 and Exercise 4.3.F(a). Keep in mind when working globally that functions give rise to natural basic open subsets.
